fields.Front: A class declares FileLogger logger; as a member and creates it itself. Which dependency pattern is this, which UML relationship, and how do you improve it?
fields.Back: Concrete + Instantiate, the worst pattern; UML composition. Improve it in two steps: extract an ILogger interface and change the member to ILogger& logger; bound by constructor injection, reaching Abstract + Inject (aggregation, DIP).

fields.Front: You need to unit-test Checkout without charging real money. Which of the four patterns makes this possible, and how?
fields.Back: Only Abstract + Inject: because Checkout holds IPaymentProcessor&, a test can inject a FakeProcessor : public IPaymentProcessor that records the call. In the other three patterns Checkout either names or creates Paypal, so you would have to edit Checkout to test it.

fields.Front: A team writes WarningLogger, InfoLogger, and FatalLogger, all printing to console with different prefixes. Diagnose and fix.
fields.Back: This is case study 1's mistake: the variation is only DATA (the prefix), not behaviour, so the subclasses are pointless. Replace all three with one ConsoleLogger(std::string level) under ILogger, configured by a constructor argument.

fields.Front: A team handles console vs database logging with an if (mode == DB) chain inside one parameterized class. Diagnose and fix.
fields.Back: The variation is BEHAVIOURAL (different algorithms), so a parameter is the wrong mechanism: it forces if-chains that grow with every new mode. Use an ILogger interface with ConsoleLogger and DatabaseLogger implementations, injected into consumers.

fields.Front: You delete virtual from ~IPaymentProcessor() and then delete a Paypal through an IPaymentProcessor*. What goes wrong?
fields.Back: Only the base destructor runs; Paypal's destructor is skipped, so any resources it holds leak (and the behaviour is formally undefined). That is why every interface in the course declares virtual ~IName() = default;.

fields.Front: You delete override from void pay(double amount) in Paypal and change the parameter to float. What happens at run time?
fields.Back: It silently becomes a NEW, unrelated function rather than an override, so Paypal stays abstract (or the base pay is called through the reference) instead of the intended behaviour. override would have turned this into a compile error.

fields.Front: You delete explicit from ConsoleLogger(std::string lvl). What newly compiles that should not?
fields.Back: Implicit conversions such as ConsoleLogger x = "DEBUG"; or passing a bare string where a ConsoleLogger is expected. explicit on single-argument constructors blocks these surprising conversions.

fields.Front: You delete the trailing const from void log(const std::string& msg) const in ConsoleLogger while ILogger keeps it. What happens?
fields.Back: It no longer overrides the base declaration (the signatures differ), so ConsoleLogger stays abstract and cannot be instantiated; with override present you get a clear compile error instead.

fields.Front: A stakeholder says 'The system must encrypt stored passwords and respond within 2 seconds, and the librarian must be able to renew a loan.' Split these into functional and non-functional.
fields.Back: Functional: 'the librarian must be able to renew a loan' (maps to a Librarian/Loan object and a renew() method). Non-functional: encryption of stored passwords (security) and the 2-second response time (performance). Anything about how well the system works is non-functional.

fields.Front: Apply the noun/verb technique to 'A librarian checks out a book to a member, and the system emails the member a due date.'
fields.Back: Nouns give candidate classes: Librarian, Book, Member, DueDate (which may end up an attribute). Verbs give candidate methods: checkOut(), email() / sendReminder(). 'Emails the member' is functional; 'within 5 seconds' would have been non-functional.

fields.Front: You must model 'Checking out a book always requires verifying membership, and overdue fines are charged only if the book is late.' Which use case relationships?
fields.Back: 'Check out book' <<include>> 'Verify membership' (always happens, arrow from base to included). 'Charge overdue fine' <<extend>> 'Return book' (optional behaviour, arrow from the extension to the base).

fields.Front: A student draws 'Michael' and 'RBC' as actors on a use case diagram. What is wrong?
fields.Back: Actors are categorical roles, not individuals: use 'Customer' (or 'Person') and 'Bank'. They must also sit outside the system boundary rectangle.

fields.Front: An Engine is destroyed when its Car is destroyed, but a Student outlives the Course object that lists them. Which UML notations do you draw?
fields.Back: Car-Engine: composition, a FILLED diamond at the Car end (strong has-a, part dies with the whole); in C++, an Engine member by value. Course-Student: aggregation, a HOLLOW diamond at the Course end; in C++, a reference or pointer member.

fields.Front: A Team must have between 5 and 11 Players, and each Player belongs to exactly one Team. What multiplicities do you write, and at which ends?
fields.Back: 1 at the Team end and 5..11 at the Player end. The number at the Player end says how many Players go with one Team; the number at the Team end says how many Teams go with one Player.

fields.Front: You draw a single arrowhead from Order to Product. What have you asserted about Product?
fields.Back: That the association is navigable only from Order to Product: Order holds a reference to its Products, but Product knows nothing about Order and has no way back.

fields.Front: Your sequence diagram must show 'if the coupon is valid apply the discount, otherwise show an error'. What do you draw?
fields.Back: An alt frame around that region, split by a dashed line into two guarded regions: [if coupon is valid] containing the discount messages, and [else] containing the error message. Exactly one region executes.

fields.Front: Someone hands you a sequence diagram containing every class in the system, drawn for a stakeholder meeting. Which named pitfalls does it hit?
fields.Back: Both: too many classes on one diagram, and making the diagram too detailed for its audience. The guidance is clarity over completeness - show one scenario clearly, at the level of detail that audience needs.
